Welcome
Mateenah is a PhD student in Community Psychology interested in in how identity, culture, critical consciousness, and community shape psychological development and sociopolitical engagement with a particular interest in queer and disabled youth of color

title: Mateenah Adeleke
text:
Beyond Research
My work in psychology is closely connected to a longstanding involvement in theatre, dance, poetry, and community-based work. I am interested in the ways creative and community spaces can shape how people understand themselves, connect with others, and navigate the worlds around them.
Learn more about me →

title: Research
text:
My research interests center on how identity, culture, social context, and critical consciousness shape psychological development and well-being. I am particularly interested in how marginalized youth and adults understand and respond to the social worlds around them, and how psychological research can better account for the cultural and structural contexts in which development occurs. Alongside these interests, I have a longstanding interest in creative expression and its potential role in psychological well-being.




As a doctoral student in the MINC Lab, I study how youth of color draw upon ethnic-racial identity and critical consciousness as resources for positive development. The lab examines how these processes shape academic engagement, STEM orientation, and activism among Black and Latinx adolescents and emerging adults.






I have worked on research examining Latine adolescents’ critical consciousness and sociopolitical engagement amid shifting political rhetoric in the United States. M



I have researched into cultural values and decolonial training among mental-health service providers to investigate how psychological services can account for cultural context and challenge assumptions embedded within conventional approaches to mental-health training.




I have quantitatively examined whether artistic expression could function as a stress-management strategy and whether personality shaped the relationship between creative coping and perceived stress.



Across these experiences, I have become increasingly interested in the intersections of identity, critical consciousness, culture, community, and psychological well-being. My current doctoral work is helping me develop these interests further, particularly in relation to youth development and sociopolitical engagement.
I am also interested in how creative practices and arts-based spaces might intersect with these processes. Rather than treating these as separate areas, I am interested in questions about how identity, culture, community, and creative expression can shape the ways young people understand themselves and their social worlds.
My research interests are continuing to develop as I engage with new theoretical perspectives, methods, and communities through my doctoral training.

title: About
text:
About Me
I grew up between the UK and Nigeria, and my early experiences moving between different communities sparked a lasting curiosity about people, culture, and the worlds we create around us.
Growing up in Hackney, London, I became involved in youth advocacy and community building through organizations including Hackney Youth Parliament, Hackney Quest, and Voyage Youth. Through these experiences, I worked with young people on community projects, youth leadership, and creating spaces where young people could have a meaningful role in shaping their neighborhoods.
The arts have been a constant thread throughout my life. I began performing spoken word and poetry after winning the Jack Petchey Speak Out Challenge, and have continued writing and performing ever since. I have also been involved in theatre facilitation with Limitless Theatre, working with children with special needs, as well as community-based poetry and arts projects. In 2026, I received the Elizabeth Babcock Poetry Prize and the Samuel A. Eliot Jr./Julia Heflin Award for Distinguished Directing in Theatre.
I completed my bachelor degree at Smith College, where I studied Psychology and Theatre. Alongside my academic work, I became involved in suicide prevention and survivor advocacy. I continue to volunteer with Impacted Survivors of Murder-Suicide.
My education and experiences have taken me across several different cultural contexts. I have had the opportunity to study and live in places including Barbados and Melbourne, Australia, experiences that have broadened the way I think about culture, community, and human experience.
These different parts of my life: psychology; the arts; community work; and experiences across cultures continue to shape how I see the world and the questions I bring to my work.
When I’m not engaged in research or community building, you can usually find me doing something connected to the arts or movement. I love dance, yoga, poetry, and theatre, and I am happiest when I have opportunities to be creative. I also love to travel. One of my ongoing personal goals is to visit every continent. (I have two more to go.)
For me, travel, art, community work, and psychology are all connected by the same underlying curiosity: people are complicated, creative, and shaped by the worlds around them. I am interested in continuing to learn from those worlds, and in finding ways to contribute to them.
